name: Dehydration cuts / water cutting

lead: Water cutting means deliberately losing body water, through water manipulation, sweating, sweat suits or saunas, to look drier and more defined for photos or events. It comes from weight-class sports such as combat sports and rowing and is borrowed by physique-focused users.
With less water under the skin, muscle and vascularity look sharper. The look is visible within hours and fades when you rehydrate. It has not been studied as a looksmaxxing method.

paras: Users change water intake and use sauna or sweat-suit sessions over hours to days before the event, then rehydrate afterward.

Sports organisations and emergency physicians have documented serious harm from extreme cuts, including several deaths of combat-sports athletes between 2015 and 2017. Regulators and physicians describe acute water loss as very dangerous, and nutrition experts generally advise against it.

chain: Drier, more defined look for a day
angle.text: Losing body water makes skin sit tighter on muscle for a drier, more defined look for a photo or event. The look shows within hours and fades on rehydration.

lead: Water cutting, or dehydration cutting, is the practice of losing body water over hours or days, typically by water manipulation, sweating, sweat suits or saunas, to weigh less or look leaner. It originates in weight-class sports such as combat sports and rowing, where athletes cut rapidly to make a weight limit.[1] In looksmaxxing and physique communities the same idea is applied to look more defined for photos or events.

Sports organisations and emergency physicians have documented serious harm from extreme cuts, including several deaths of combat-sports athletes between 2015 and 2017.[1] Nutrition experts rarely advise on how to do it safely and generally recommend against it.[1]
infobox: Water manipulation, sweating, sweat suits, saunas[1]

paras: Weight cutting can involve losing fat and muscle over weeks, or losing water in the final days before weigh-in.[1] The water-loss form is the one popularly called water cutting; reported methods include water loading, food restriction, exercise sweating, sweat suits and saunas.[1]

sections.h: Use in sport and physique culture
paras: Combat-sport athletes often cut to compete in a lower weight class, rehydrating between weigh-in and the bout.[1] Physique-oriented communities describe temporary water loss as a way to reduce a soft or puffy look for a short window; no community threads were reviewed for this article.

In December 2015, a 21-year-old Chinese MMA fighter, Yang Jian Bing, died while cutting weight for a ONE Championship bout; the promotion subsequently banned dehydration-based cuts, moved to walking-weight arrangements and added urine specific gravity testing.[1] Muay Thai fighters Jordan Coe (March 2016) and Jessica Lindsay (November 2017) also died after cuts.[1] An emergency physician has called acute water loss very dangerous and urged hydration testing.[1]

In 2022 the Mohegan Tribe Department of Athletic Regulation suspended a fighter for six months and fined him after he posted video of himself vomiting during a cut.[1] A 2013 IOC-linked position statement addressed minimising health risks in weight-sensitive sports.[1]
No studies found on cosmetic dehydration cuts specifically. Research on weight-cutting methods in athletes exists, including a 2019 survey of self-reported methods among professional MMA athletes.[1]

lore.intro: Water cutting is discussed in physique circles as a short-term way to look drier or leaner; the claims below reflect that general framing rather than specific threads.

claims.claim: Dropping water makes you look more shredded for a day.
Water cuts are safe if done briefly.
